body_text: BACK TO NEWSROOM Getty Images Getty Images to Release Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results on August 10, 2026 Jul 23, 2026 | PDF New York‑July 23, 2026: Getty Images Holdings, Inc. (“Getty Images”) (NYSE: GETY) a preeminent global visual content creator and marketplace, announced today that the Company intends to release its second quarter 2026 results after market close on Monday, August 10, 2026, followed by a conference call at 4:30 p.m. (Eastern Time) that same day. The call will consist of prepared remarks only. The conference call can be accessed live over the phone by dialing 1‑833‑309‑3473, or for international callers, 1‑785‑838‑9251. The conference ID for the call is GETTY. An audio replay will be available for two weeks following the call and can be accessed by dialing 1‑844‑512‑2921, or for international callers, 1‑412‑317‑6671. The passcode for the replay is 11162213. A simultaneous webcast of the conference call will also be available on the Investor Relations section of the Company’s website at https://investors.gettyimages.com/ . The webcast will also be available for replay shortly following the call. About Getty Images: Getty Images (NYSE: GETY) is a preeminent global visual content creator and marketplace that offers a full range of content solutions to meet the needs of any customer around the globe, no matter their size. Through its Getty Images , iStock and Unsplash brands, websites and APIs, Getty Images serves customers in almost every country in the world and is the first‑place people turn to discover, purchase and share powerful visual content from the world’s best photographers and videographers. Getty Images works with over 600,000 content creators and over 360 content partners to deliver this powerful and comprehensive content. Each year Getty Images covers more than 160,000 news , sport and entertainment events providing depth and breadth of coverage that is unmatched. Getty Images maintains one of the largest and best privately‑owned photographic archives in the world with millions of images dating back to the beginning of photography. Through its best‑in‑class creative library and Custom Content solutions, Getty Images helps customers elevate their creativity and entire end‑to‑end creative process to find the right visual for any need. With the adoption and distribution of generative AI technologies and tools trained on permissioned content that include indemnification and perpetual, worldwide usage rights, Getty Images and iStock customers can use text to image generation to ideate and create commercially safe compelling visuals, further expanding Getty Images capabilities to deliver exactly what customers are looking for. For company news and announcements, visit our Newsroom . title: Collections Strategy for High-PPO Dental Practices
body_text: A high PPO dental collections strategy is a systematic approach to maximizing revenue in dental practices that accept multiple PPO insurance plans. It combines insurance billing optimization, proactive accounts receivable management, and front-end scheduling coverage to achieve a 98%+ net collection rate — the benchmark for collecting at least 98 cents of every dollar legally owed after PPO contractual write-offs are applied. The best high PPO dental collections strategy for 2026 combines three disciplines: insurance billing optimization, proactive AR follow-up, and front-end scheduling coverage. High-performing PPO practices collect 98%+ of net production by verifying insurance before every appointment, submitting same-day claims, working denials within 30 days, and closing the scheduling gaps that keep production out of the revenue cycle. Running a high-PPO practice is a calculated trade-off. You accept contracted write-offs in exchange for patient volume. The danger is when write-offs compound on top of billing errors, aging receivables, and missed calls — turning a volume strategy into a cash flow problem. This guide covers a complete high PPO dental collections strategy for 2026. It starts with your true write-off baseline, moves through fee schedule renegotiation, and closes with the scheduling gaps that quietly drain revenue. High-PPO practices face contractual write-offs before billing begins. Denials compound the margin squeeze. Missed calls keep production from entering the revenue cycle at all. The highest-leverage fixes: verify insurance 48-72 hours before appointments, submit claims same-day, work denials within 30 days, and collect patient portions before patients leave. Renegotiate fee schedules every two years. Billing fixes alone aren't enough. Thirty-five percent of dental calls go unanswered on average — production that's never scheduled never enters AR. This guide covers the full cycle, front end to back end. Key Takeaways Billing and AR: Track net collection rate, not gross — PPO write-offs make gross rates misleading; high-performing PPO practices target 98%+ on net collected vs. net production, per dental billing KPI benchmarks . 85%+ of AR should be under 30 days — accounts older than 90 days have less than a 50% chance of being collected , making speed-to-submit the highest-leverage billing habit. 15-20% of dental claims are denied on first submission — but practices with structured pre-verification programs consistently report significant reductions in denial rates, with industry estimates suggesting improvements of 25–50% depending on baseline processes. Most PPO practices never renegotiate fee schedules — major insurers allow renegotiation every two years, and successful negotiations can meaningfully increase reimbursement revenue. Scheduling and Patient Communication: 35% of dental calls go unanswered on average — each missed new patient call represents an average of $850 in immediate revenue loss and potentially $4,500+ over the patient lifetime. Close patient financial conversations before treatment begins — patients who receive an accurate cost estimate upfront pay faster and dispute less. Integrating AI-powered patient communication alongside your billing systems recovers production at both ends of the revenue cycle: scheduling and collections. What Makes a High-PPO Collections Strategy Different? High-PPO dental practices operate under a fundamentally different financial model than fee-for-service or membership-plan practices. Understanding the difference is the prerequisite for building a collections strategy that actually fits your environment. How PPO Write-Offs Change the Math In a PPO-heavy practice, every billable procedure starts with a contractual write-off — the difference between your full fee and the contracted reimbursement rate. PPO write-offs average 20-35% per contracted procedure depending on the plan and your fee schedule, according to industry benchmarks from Dentx . For a practice producing $1 million annually with 50% PPO patients, that translates to $100,000-$175,000 in contractual adjustments before you've seen a single billing error. Three Challenges Unique to PPO-Heavy Practices This creates three challenges that don't exist at the same scale in fee-for-service practices: Lower margins require higher volume — a $250 crown that reimbursed at $180 needs to be scheduled, staffed, and billed at the same cost as one that reimbursed at $250. Missed production, unbilled procedures, and avoidable write-offs hit harder. Gross collection rates become misleading — your gross rate reflects contractual write-offs as if they were collection failures. High-PPO practices must track net collection rate (amount collected vs. amount legally collectible after contractual adjustments) to get an accurate picture of billing health. Insurance dependency creates administrative overhead — verifying plans, submitting clean claims, managing denials, and tracking plan-specific billing rules is significantly more complex when you participate in 8-12 PPO contracts simultaneously. The strategies in this guide are designed specifically for this context: maximizing revenue within the PPO model rather than simply benchmarking against fee-for-service norms. Why Do High-PPO Practices Leave Revenue on the Table? The PPO model was designed to trade margin for volume. What most practices don't account for is the compounding of losses that occurs when both ends of the revenue cycle are leaking simultaneously — back-end billing errors AND front-end scheduling gaps. The Back-End Leak: Billing, Denials, and Patient AR Most high-PPO practices focus their improvement effort on the AR side: billing accuracy, denial rates, patient balance follow-up. Those matter. But the data on dental practice phone coverage reveals a second, often larger leak hiding in plain sight: The Front-End Leak: Missed Calls and Unscheduled Production Dental practices miss an average of 35% of inbound calls , with some practices reporting missing well over half of calls during peak hours, per Resonate's missed call research Only 14% of patients leave a voicemail when a call goes unanswered — the rest move on to the next in-network provider A practice missing 10 new patient calls per month loses approximately $8,500/month in immediate production — over $100,000 annually — before a single billing error is counted Production that was never scheduled never enters the billing cycle at all — no claim to file, no AR to manage, no collection to attempt The practices that outperform on PPO collections benchmarks address both ends. Back end: billing accuracy, AR discipline, and fee negotiation. Front end: reliable call coverage , patient communication, and scheduling efficiency. This guide covers both, in the order they occur in your revenue cycle. Calculate Your True PPO Write-Off Baseline Before you can improve collections, you need an accurate picture of where production is going. Most PPO practices track overall production and overall collections. But that aggregate view masks which contracts are genuinely profitable and which are eroding margin faster than they generate volume. Dental PPO write-offs, analyzed by contract, reveal the specific plans driving the most margin compression. Run a Contract-Level Write-Off Analysis Pull your write-offs by PPO contract for the past 12 months. For each plan, calculate: Contracted reimbursement rate vs. your UCR (Usual, Customary, and Reasonable) fee Net production per plan — production minus contractual write-offs Volume per plan — number of patients and procedures billed to that payer Denial rate per plan — claims denied on first submission Effective collected rate per plan — amount paid vs. amount legally collectable after write-offs This analysis frequently reveals that 2-3 contracts account for a disproportionate share of write-offs relative to volume. You cannot make good decisions about which PPO relationships to maintain, renegotiate, or exit without this baseline. Establish Your Net Collection Rate Target For PPO practices, the target is a 98%+ net collection rate — meaning you collect at least 98% of everything you're contractually entitled to after write-offs are applied, per Dentx's collection benchmarks . A practice at 93% net collection and one at 98% net collection look identical on gross production. But the 98% practice collects $50,000 more each year — on the same volume, with no additional patients. Track the Right AR Aging Metrics The standard AR aging benchmarks for a healthy dental practice are: AR Aging Targets Table AR Aging Bucket Healthy Target 0–30 days 85%+ of total AR 31–60 days Under 10% 61–90 days Under 5% Over 90 days Under 2% Total AR Days Under 30 (18–24 for top practices) Source: Dental AR Benchmarking — Pearly PPO Collections KPIs at a Glance Revenue Cycle Performance Metrics Table Metric High-Performing Target Needs Attention Critical Net Collection Rate 98%+ 95–97% Below 95% AR Days Outstanding 18–24 days 25–35 days Over 35 days AR Over 30 Days Under 15% of total AR 15–25% Over 25% AR Over 90 Days Under 2% of total AR 2–5% Over 5% First-Pass Claim Rate 95%+ 85–94% Below 85% Denial Rate Under 5% 5–15% Over 15% Missed Call Rate Under 10% 10–25% Over 25% Industry benchmarks sourced from Dental Billing Assist Once a receivable passes 90 days, the probability of collection drops below 50%, according to dental billing KPI benchmarks . Managing PPO dental accounts receivable against these thresholds is essential. For PPO practices already working on thinner margins, aged receivables compound the problem. You've delivered the care, accepted the write-off — and still can't collect the patient portion. Pro Tip: Review your AR aging dashboard weekly, not monthly. Monthly reviews mean 4-5 weeks pass before you notice a claim aging past 30 days — by then, denial appeal windows may have closed. Verify Insurance Before Every Appointment Insurance verification is the highest-leverage habit in PPO billing. It prevents denials before they happen, gives patients an accurate cost estimate before treatment, and eliminates the billing delays that cause AR to age. Practices that automate pre-appointment insurance verification run eligibility checks for every scheduled appointment. No manual overhead added to the front desk. What Verification Actually Means for PPO Patients Verification for PPO patients goes beyond confirming active coverage. A complete pre-appointment verification checks: Coverage basics: Active eligibility — is the patient still covered under this plan? Annual maximum remaining — how much is left in the benefit year? Deductible status — has the deductible been met, and how much is remaining? Coverage percentages by procedure code — what does the plan actually pay for the scheduled procedure? Plan-specific rules: Frequency limitations — has this procedure already been performed within the plan's limitation window? Waiting periods — are there any waiting periods that apply to the planned treatment? Coordination of benefits — does the patient have a secondary plan, and what is the COB structure? Plan-specific billing rules — downgrades, missing tooth clauses, alternative benefit policies Missing any of these items — especially frequency limitations and plan-specific rules — is among the most common sources of preventable claim denials for PPO practices. The Financial Impact of Structured Verification The data on verification impact is clear: Practices with structured pre-appointment verification programs consistently report significant reductions in claim denial rates — industry estimates range from 25% to 50% improvement depending on baseline processes First-pass claim acceptance rates improve meaningfully in the first month of structured verification implementation 15-20% of dental insurance claims are denied on first submission industry-wide; that number drops significantly for practices that verify before the appointment rather than during billing Pro Tip: Build verification into your scheduling workflow, not your billing workflow. Verification done three days before the appointment gives your team time to contact the patient with accurate cost estimates — verification done the morning of the appointment is too late to change anything. Submit Clean Claims on Day One Every day between service delivery and claim submission adds a day to your AR cycle. For PPO practices managing high claim volume, same-day submission is the single practice that most directly compresses AR days. What a Clean Claim Requires A clean claim is one submitted with all required information, correct coding, and proper documentation — in the format the payer expects. For PPO practices, clean claim requirements include: Clinical accuracy: CDT coding accuracy — billing the most specific code that accurately describes the procedure. Over-coding creates audit risk; under-coding leaves reimbursement on the table. CDT coding accuracy alone often recovers thousands of dollars annually in lost reimbursement. Radiograph and charting attachments — many PPO plans require x-rays for specific procedures. Missing attachments on submission are among the most common reasons for pended claims, per Dental Claim Support . Accurate tooth numbers and surfaces — claim rejections from simple data entry errors are 100% preventable Administrative completeness: Correct claim form fields — provider NPI, tax ID, place of service, and date of service all need to match what's on file with the payer Secondary claim coordination — if a patient has dual coverage, file the primary claim first, then use the EOB to file the secondary claim Pro Tip: Build a same-day claims checklist into your end-of-day huddle. Identify which procedures were completed, confirm all documentation is attached in the PMS, and submit before closing. Claims filed after 5 PM Monday-Friday have identical processing timelines to claims filed the next morning — there's no benefit to waiting. Why 65% of Denied Claims Never Get Resubmitted Bandwidth is almost always the root cause: when the front desk manages verification, check-in, scheduling, and claims simultaneously, denial follow-up is the first task to slip. Dental billing industry data consistently estimates that 60-65% of denied claims are never resubmitted — permanent revenue loss for PPO practices already operating on compressed margins. You've delivered the service, accepted the write-off, and forfeited the remaining reimbursement because a denial went unworked. The strategies in the next section address this directly. Build a Proactive AR Follow-Up System Denial and AR follow-up is the most common breakdown point in high-PPO billing systems. The volume of claims is high, each plan has different timely filing limits and appeal processes, and the administrative workload in dental practices competes directly with patient-facing tasks. A 30/60/90-Day Follow-Up Framework Structure your AR follow-up around aging milestones: 0-30 Days (Insurance) Submit claims same-day Confirm receipt for all electronic submissions by Day 3 Flag any non-acknowledgments for resubmission by Day 7 Work any denials immediately — appeal windows are typically 30-90 days from the denial date 30-60 Days (Insurance + Patient) Pull aging report and identify any claims still pending after 30 days Call payer or check portal for claim status on all pending claims Send first patient statement for any patient portion not collected at checkout Add automated billing reminder for any open patient balance 60-90 Days (Escalation) Personal outreach for any patient balance over $100 that hasn't responded to statements Submit formal appeals for all denied claims within payer's appeal window Escalate any insurance claim past 60 days to a dedicated billing follow-up call Over 90 Days (Recovery Mode) Review for timely filing — many PPO plans have 90-180 day timely filing limits Escalate to secondary collections process for patient balances over $200 Write off only after exhausting all appeal and collection options — and document the reason Build Denial Tracking Into Your PMS Workflow Every PMS platform — whether you're on OpenDental , EagleSoft, Dentrix, or Denticon — has denial tracking and AR aging report features. The problem isn't tool availability, it's process: many PPO practices check these reports reactively rather than scheduling a daily denial review. Daily AR habits that protect PPO collections: Morning: Pull yesterday's EOB postings and identify any new denials Weekly: Run a full aging report and review all claims over 30 days Monthly: Review net collection rate by insurance plan and by provider Set Up Patient Financial Conversations Before Treatment Patient balances are the most difficult collections category for PPO practices. Once a patient has left the office, collection rates drop significantly — statements generate lower response rates than at-checkout conversations, and patients dispute balances they don't understand. The solution is financial transparency before treatment, not after. The Pre-Treatment Financial Conversation For every treatment with a patient portion above $100, the front desk or treatment coordinator should provide: A written cost estimate — broken down by procedure, expected insurance payment, and patient responsibility Confirmation that benefits were verified — "We've checked your Delta Dental plan, and here's what we found..." A clear payment expectation — "Your portion for today's crown is expected to be $320. We'll collect that at checkout today." Payment options — in-house payment plan, CareCredit, FSA/HSA accepted, card on file Pro Tip: "Expected" language is important. Insurance estimates are never guarantees — using language like "based on your current benefits, your estimated portion is $320" protects you legally and sets realistic expectations. Why Upfront Financial Conversations Reduce Bad Debt Patients who are surprised by a bill after the fact dispute more and pay more slowly. When a patient understands their cost responsibility before treatment and verbally agrees to it, three things happen: Fewer disputes — the bill matches what they expected Faster payment — they budgeted for it before the appointment Better collection rate on patient balances — dental industry data consistently shows that day-of collection rates are significantly higher than post-statement collection rates, as patients are more likely to pay before they leave the office For PPO practices, patient cost-sharing after write-offs can still run $100-$500+ per procedure. That makes collection timing a real revenue variable — not an administrative preference. Practices focused on improving patient retention rates find clear financial communication is one of the highest-leverage habits available. Patients who understand their bill upfront pay faster and dispute less. Renegotiate Your PPO Fee Schedules Every Two Years One of the most underpracticed strategies in high-PPO dental billing is fee schedule negotiation. Most practices accept the rates they received at enrollment and never revisit them. Major insurers allow renegotiation every two years. Most practices never start the conversation. What Fee Negotiation Can Return Successful PPO fee schedule negotiations raise reimbursement rates on your highest-volume CDT codes — adding revenue on the same patient base, with no additional patients required. According to Apex Reimbursement Specialists , even modest rate improvements on high-volume CDT codes translate to meaningful recovered production. How to Approach PPO Renegotiation Step 1: Audit your current fee schedules For each PPO contract, compare your UCR fee to the contracted reimbursement on your highest-volume CDT codes. Identify the widest gaps — these are your negotiation targets. Step 2: Raise your UCR fees annually Insurers typically base renegotiation offers on your UCR fee schedule. Practices that haven't raised their UCR in 3+ years have less negotiating leverage. Increase your UCR by at least 3% annually — this signals to payers that your market rate is rising, and it sets a higher baseline for the negotiation. Step 3: Prepare a data-driven case Document your patient volume per plan Calculate your effective collected rate after write-offs Show how the current fee schedule compares to your practice costs Cite regional UCR data if available Step 4: Leverage patient volume Insurance companies want to keep high-volume providers in-network. A practice with 1,200 active patients on a plan has real leverage. Losing that provider disrupts care access for their members. Per Veritas Dental Resources , patient volume is one of the strongest negotiation tools you have. Step 5: Consider a PPO negotiation specialist Due to the complexity involved, many practices partner with a third-party PPO negotiation firm that specializes in navigating insurer policies and advocating on your behalf. The cost of a specialist is typically offset by the first month of improved reimbursement. Close the Scheduling Gaps That Drain Collections PPO billing systems and AR management address the back-end of the revenue cycle. But there's a front-end collections leak that most PPO practices overlook: missed calls and after-hours scheduling gaps that prevent production from being scheduled in the first place. For high-PPO practices, every empty appointment slot is a complete production loss — you've built the overhead for the volume model, and the revenue simply doesn't arrive. The Missed Call Revenue Problem The numbers on missed calls in dental practices are striking: Dental practices miss an average of 35% of incoming calls , with some practices reporting missing well over half of calls during peak hours, per Resonate's missed call research and Arini's research on missed call rates in dental practices Most new patients call before their first visit — and only 14% leave a voicemail if unanswered, per dental industry surveys — meaning the vast majority of missed new patient calls are gone permanently A practice missing just 10 new patient calls per month loses approximately $8,500/month in immediate revenue, or over $100,000 annually — and that's before accounting for patient lifetime value of $4,500+ per patient For a high-PPO practice that depends on volume to make the model work, missing new patient calls is a direct hit to the collections baseline. Every call that goes unanswered is scheduled production that never happens — no claim is filed, no collection is attempted, no AR is generated. The revenue simply never enters the cycle. Pro Tip: Track your missed call rate from your PMS or phone system analytics. If your practice misses more than 10% of inbound calls during business hours, phone coverage is a collections issue, not just a front desk issue. See Arini's guide on improving missed call percentage in dental offices for a breakdown of when and why calls go unanswered. After-Hours Scheduling: The Silent Revenue Gap A significant portion of patient scheduling intent happens outside business hours. Patients research practices, get motivated to book, and attempt to schedule at 7 PM or on a Saturday morning — and reach voicemail. Per-call data from Arini's AI receptionist platform shows that after-hours call volume for dental practices is substantial, particularly for new patients who are comparison-shopping between in-network providers. For high-PPO practices where patients are actively looking for in-network providers, after-hours availability is a competitive differentiator. The practice that answers at 8 PM books the patient; the practice that takes a voicemail loses them to a practice with 24/7 coverage. Tools and Solutions That Extend Your Collections Strategy A high-PPO collections strategy requires two categories of tools working in parallel: billing and AR management systems, and patient communication and scheduling systems. The most common gap in PPO practices is the second category. Your PMS Billing and AR Toolkit Your practice management software — whether OpenDental, EagleSoft , Dentrix, Denticon, or another platform — is the foundation. These systems handle: Claim submission and electronic remittance posting AR aging reports and denial tracking Fee schedule management and write-off tracking Insurance verification integrations (through third-party clearinghouses) The key is configuring these systems to enforce the workflows described in this guide: same-day submission, pre-appointment verification, AR aging alerts, and denial follow-up queues. The tools are available in every major PMS — the bottleneck is process, not software. While your billing team manages the back-end AR and insurance workflow, Arini's AI receptionist handles the patient-facing communication layer that ensures production is scheduled and confirmed before it ever reaches billing. Arini integrates directly with your PMS so every inbound call — during business hours, over lunch, and after hours — converts to a booked appointment with verified patient data ready for your billing team. Best Practices Summary Back-End: Billing, AR, and Fee Schedules Verify every patient's insurance 48-72 hours before their appointment — not the morning of Submit all claims the same day as service delivery — daily end-of-day claim submission is non-negotiable Track net collection rate by insurance plan — not just gross collection across all payers Review AR aging weekly, not monthly — denial appeal windows close fast, and aging compounds Have financial conversations before treatment, not after — day-of collection rates are significantly higher than post-statement rates Never let a denial go unworked past 30 days — 65% of denied claims that go unworked become permanent write-offs Fee Strategy and Front-End Revenue: Audit PPO write-offs by contract annually — identify which plans are genuinely profitable at your patient volume Renegotiate fee schedules every two years — most practices never initiate; those that do recover significant reimbursement Raise UCR fees annually — gives you negotiation leverage and reflects real market rate increases Close after-hours phone gaps — production that isn't scheduled never enters the collections cycle Common Mistakes Metric and verification mistakes: Tracking gross collection rate in a PPO-heavy practice — contractual write-offs make gross rates misleading; net collection rate is the correct metric Skipping verification for returning patients — benefits change at annual renewal; a patient verified in January may have a completely different plan by July Waiting until billing time to verify insurance — verification done after the patient has already been in the chair serves no purpose for patient communication Claims submission mistakes: Filing secondary claims manually after primary EOB — many practices delay secondary billing by 30+ days; it should happen within 48 hours of receiving primary EOB Accepting the first denial without appealing — many denials on first submission are administrative, not clinical. Clean up the claim and resubmit. AR Oversight and Scheduling Mistakes: Not working AR follow-up until month-end — monthly AR reviews mean claims can age 45+ days before anyone notices Writing off aged balances without documenting the reason — untracked write-offs obscure your true net collection rate and make it impossible to identify systemic billing problems Not tracking missed calls as a revenue metric — if your practice misses 30% of inbound calls, that's a collections problem that billing systems can't solve Final Verdict There's no single fix that solves high-PPO collections — it's a full-cycle problem that requires attention at both ends of the revenue pipeline. Here's how to prioritize based on where your practice stands: Back-end billing fixes first: If your net collection rate is below 95% , start with back-end billing: verification timing, same-day claims, and structured denial follow-up. These typically produce the most immediate gains. If your AR aging shows more than 15% over 60 days , denial follow-up bandwidth is the bottleneck. Assign ownership and escalate claims past 30 days the same week — not at month-end. Fee schedule and front-end fixes next: If you've never renegotiated your PPO fee schedules , that's a missed two-year opportunity. Start with your highest-volume plans — the data you need is already in your PMS. If your practice misses more than 10% of inbound calls , the front-end leak is outpacing what billing improvements can recover. No AR discipline or fee negotiation compensates for production that was never scheduled. For the scheduling and patient communication side of the equation, Arini's AI receptionist integrates with your PMS and provides 24/7 call coverage — so every new patient call converts to a booked appointment and every scheduled appointment enters the billing cycle with complete insurance data already captured. Book a Demo Frequently Asked Questions What Net Collection Rate Should PPO Practices Target? High-performing PPO dental practices target a 98%+ net collection rate — meaning they collect at least 98% of everything they're legally entitled to collect after contractual write-offs are applied. A rate below 95% typically indicates billing process gaps: missed claim submissions, unworked denials, or insufficient patient balance follow-up. Track net rate by plan to identify which PPO contracts are dragging your overall rate down. How do I calculate PPO write-off percentage? For each PPO contract, divide total contractual write-offs by total production billed to that plan, then multiply by 100. For example: $75,000 in write-offs on $250,000 in production to that plan equals a 30% write-off rate. Run this calculation per plan, per year — not in aggregate — so you can see which contracts are generating disproportionate write-offs relative to patient volume. How often should dental AR be reviewed? Ideally, you should pull a denial report daily and an AR aging report weekly . Monthly reviews are insufficient for PPO practices with high claim volume — by the time you notice a claim aging past 45 days in a monthly review, you may have missed the payer's denial appeal window. Best-practice PPO billing teams assign someone to review new denials every morning and hold a weekly AR meeting to work the 30-60-90 day aging buckets. Can I renegotiate my PPO fee schedule? Yes. Major dental insurers allow PPO fee schedule renegotiation approximately every two years. Most practices never initiate the process, but those that do can achieve meaningful reimbursement improvements. Your strongest negotiating leverage is patient volume — high-volume providers are harder for insurers to lose from their network. Start by raising your UCR fees annually and preparing a contract-level data analysis before requesting a renegotiation meeting. What Is the Biggest Hidden Revenue Leak in PPO Practices? Missed calls are the most underappreciated revenue leak in PPO practices. Practices miss an average of 35% of inbound calls — and most new patients call before scheduling, but only 14% leave a voicemail if unanswered, per dental industry research. For a PPO practice that depends on volume, every missed new patient call is scheduled production that never enters the revenue cycle. No billing system can recover revenue from an appointment that was never booked. See how Arini's AI receptionist eliminates missed calls for dental practices running at high PPO participation. How does insurance verification reduce claim denials? Plan-specific billing rules — downgrades, missing tooth clauses, and alternative benefit policies — are among the most practice-specific denial triggers and vary significantly across PPO contracts. title: 10 Essential SRE Metrics for Reliable Systems
summary: Discover the 10 essential SRE metrics that ensure system reliability. Learn how to implement and leverage these metrics for optimal performance.
body_text: 10 Essential SRE Metrics for Reliable Systems Published on: December 19, 2024 Last Updated: July 02, 2026 18 min read Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) metrics guide your system's performance and reliability. In the fast-paced world of DevOps, success begins with effective monitoring. By blending software development with IT operations, SRE builds resilient, scalable systems that balance speed with reliability. SRE ensures visibility into system health and performance through data-driven metrics and cross-team collaboration. As systems grow more complex, accurate, actionable metrics become essential. But which metrics truly matter? And how can they be implemented effectively? This guide dives into these questions, equipping you with the tools to enhance reliability and take your systems to the next level. What are SRE Metrics and Why Are They Important? Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is a discipline that bridges software development and IT operations, applying engineering principles to improve system reliability, scalability, and efficiency. At its core, SRE focuses on automation, observability, and continuous improvement to ensure seamless operations. SRE metrics are quantifiable measures that provide actionable insights into a system’s health, performance, and reliability. They serve as critical tools for identifying potential issues, guiding proactive management, and driving informed decision-making. Why Are SRE Metrics Crucial? Objective Insights: Enable teams to rely on data, not intuition, for decision-making. Proactive Management: Highlight potential risks before they impact end users. Continuous Improvement: Track the effectiveness of changes and optimizations over time. Business Alignment: Directly correlate technical performance with user experience and business outcomes. By fostering a data-driven culture, SRE metrics empower teams to communicate effectively and prioritize reliability without compromising development speed. This approach has been popularized by companies like Google, where SRE originated in 2003 under Ben Treynor, who described it as: “What happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations function.” Modern SRE practices leverage tools to monitor Service-Level Indicators (SLIs), Service-Level Objectives (SLOs), and Service-Level Agreements (SLAs)—the pillars of measuring system reliability. By embedding these metrics into DevOps workflows, organizations can better navigate the complexities of distributed systems and ensure long-term resilience. The Four Golden Signals: Foundation of SRE Metrics Google's SRE team introduced the concept of Four Golden Signals — a set of metrics that provide a holistic view of system health. These signals form the cornerstone of effective SRE practices: The four golden Signals Latency: How long does it take to serve a request? Traffic: How many requests is your system handling? Errors: How often do requests fail? Saturation: How close is your system to its capacity? Let's dive deeper into each of these signals: Latency Latency measures the time it takes for a system to respond to a request. High latency can frustrate users and lead to churn, especially in applications like e-commerce or streaming, where speed is crucial. Latency Imagine a streaming service with latency exceeding 3 seconds. Users may perceive buffering as a failure, leading to subscription cancellations. It's critical to monitor average latency and focus on percentiles (e.g., 95th or 99th) to capture edge cases that affect user experience. Key Considerations: Measure both successful and failed requests separately, as failures can skew the average. Use percentiles (e.g., 95th or 99th) instead of averages to capture a more accurate range of user experiences. Establish baselines and thresholds based on application type and user expectations. Tools & Implementation: SigNoz: Set up latency metrics for your endpoints and visualize trends with real-time dashboards. SigNoz offers detailed insights into transaction latency, allowing you to track both average and percentile latency for various endpoints. New Relic or DataDog: Monitor transaction-level latency in real-time. Configure alerts for thresholds like response times exceeding 500ms for critical endpoints. Correlate latency spikes with other metrics like traffic or saturation to diagnose root causes. Example: A surge in latency during peak traffic might reveal the need for database query optimization or scaling. Traffic Traffic reflects the volume of demand on your system, such as API requests or active users. Monitoring traffic helps identify trends, anticipate scaling needs, and detect anomalies like traffic surges due to DDoS attacks or misconfigurations. A sudden 5x increase in API requests during a flash sale could crash the system without adequate preparation. Understanding traffic patterns allows teams to plan capacity and maintain uptime during such spikes. Key Considerations: Define what "traffic" means for your system—this could range from API calls to active user sessions. Monitor real-time and historical traffic to detect usage patterns and anomalies. Use monitoring tools like Prometheus or Datadog to correlate traffic with latency and saturation, identifying how rising demand impacts system performance. This helps pinpoint bottlenecks, such as CPU limits or database locks, and enables optimized scaling and resource allocation to prevent degradation. Tools & Implementation: SigNoz: Monitor traffic, latency, and errors with integrated dashboards that provide actionable insights into system performance. Grafana Dashboards: Visualize request rates and identify peak times. Google Cloud Monitoring: Analyze historical traffic trends for capacity planning. AWS Auto Scaling: Configure autoscaling for application servers based on traffic data. PagerDuty: Receive real-time alerts when traffic surges are detected. Example: Configuring autoscaling for application servers based on traffic patterns ensures your system adapts to demand fluctuations. Auto-Scaling Auto-Scaling Errors Errors track the rate of failed requests, whether they’re caused by server-side issues (500-level errors), client errors (400-level), or third-party integrations. Monitoring errors helps teams prioritize fixes and maintain user trust. A 5% error rate in payment gateway requests can lead to significant revenue loss and user dissatisfaction. Categorizing errors (e.g., payment failures vs. UI glitches) helps in prioritizing resolutions effectively. Error Rate Error Rate Key Considerations: Categorize errors (e.g., client-side, server-side, or third-party dependency failures). Set up error budgets to balance reliability with feature delivery velocity. Use logs and metrics to pinpoint failure causes and prioritize fixes. Tools & Implementation: ELK Stack or Splunk: Aggregate and analyze logs to pinpoint error causes. Sentry: Track errors in real time and alert teams with detailed stack traces. Set error budgets (e.g., <2% errors per month ) to align reliability with development velocity. Implement automated retries for transient errors and configure alerts for consistent spikes in failures. Example: Integrating automated incident response workflows for error spikes can significantly reduce downtime. Saturation Saturation measures resource usage, such as CPU, memory, and disk space, relative to their capacity. Overloaded resources can lead to degraded performance or system crashes. A database server operating at 90% disk I/O capacity may slow down application queries, causing latency spikes and failed transactions. Proactive monitoring of saturation can prevent such issues. Saturation Saturation Key Considerations: Track key resources like CPU, memory, disk throughput, and network bandwidth. Proactively set thresholds for resource usage to prevent degradation before reaching full capacity. Monitor saturation trends to anticipate scaling needs. Tools & Implementation: Nagios or CloudWatch: Monitor CPU, memory, and storage metrics. Set resource utilization thresholds (e.g., 80% for CPU or memory). Use Kubernetes HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) to scale resources dynamically. Create dashboards to track saturation alongside latency and traffic for a holistic view. Example: Scaling up a database cluster during high write operations ensures consistent performance under load. How to Implement the Four Golden Signals Implementing the Four Golden Signals requires a systematic approach: Choose the right tools: Select monitoring and observability platforms that can collect and visualize these metrics effectively. Instrument your code: Add appropriate logging and metric collection points throughout your application. Set baselines: Establish normal operating ranges for each metric based on historical data. Configure alerts: Create alerting rules that trigger when metrics deviate significantly from baselines. Integrate with incident management: Ensure that alerts are routed to the appropriate teams and tied into your incident response workflows. Visualize data: Create dashboards that provide at-a-glance views of system health based on these signals. Remember, the goal is not just to collect data, but to make it actionable. Regular reviews and refinements of your metrics and alerting strategies are essential. Beyond the Golden Signals: Additional SRE Metrics While the Four Golden Signals provide a solid foundation, additional metrics can offer deeper insights into your system's reliability: Availability Availability measures the percentage of time your system is operational and accessible to users. It's often expressed as a number of nines (e.g., 99.9% uptime). Availability directly impacts user trust and business reputation. High availability ensures minimal disruption, especially for mission-critical applications. To calculate availability: Availability = ( Total Time - Downtime ) / Total Time * 100 Set clear Service Level Objectives (SLOs) for availability and track your performance against these targets. Throughput Throughput measures the rate at which your system processes requests. It's closely related to traffic but focuses on the system's output rather than input. Monitoring throughput helps teams assess system performance under varying loads, ensuring scalability and optimal resource allocation. Key considerations for throughput: Measure in relevant units (e.g., requests per second, transactions per minute). Monitor trends to identify capacity needs and performance improvements. Correlate with resource utilization to optimize efficiency. Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) MTTD measures how quickly you become aware of issues in your system. Reducing MTTD is crucial for minimizing the impact of incidents. Reducing MTTD minimizes the impact of system failures by enabling faster incident resolution. To understand MTTD, have a look at the below example: Consider three incidents: Incident 1: Occurred at 8:00 AM, detected at 8:30 AM (30 minutes). Incident 2: Occurred at 3:00 PM, detected at 3:20 PM (20 minutes). Incident 3: Occurred at 11:00 PM, detected at 12:00 AM (60 minutes). Calculation: This means, on average, issues were detected within 36.67 minutes, highlighting the monitoring system’s efficiency. To improve MTTD: Implement comprehensive monitoring and alerting. Use anomaly detection and AI-powered analytics. Foster a culture of vigilance and quick communication. Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR) MTTR tracks how long it takes to resolve issues once they're detected. It's a key indicator of your team's incident response effectiveness. Lower MTTR reflects a team's efficiency in mitigating downtime and restoring normalcy, which is vital for customer satisfaction. Strategies to reduce MTTR: Develop and refine incident response playbooks. For example, create a database outage playbook that includes steps for failing over to a replica and notifying stakeholders. Implement automation for common remediation tasks. For instance, automatically restart a crashed service when CPU utilization exceeds a defined threshold. Conduct thorough post-mortems to prevent recurring issues. For example, after a server crash caused by memory leaks, deploy monitoring to alert the team when memory usage spikes. Change Failure Rate This metric measures the percentage of changes (e.g., deployments, updates) that result in degraded service or require remediation. A lower change failure rate indicates a more robust development pipeline and fewer disruptions due to updates. To use change failure rate effectively: Track all changes and their outcomes. Analyze failures to identify common causes. Use the insights to improve your development and deployment processes. How to Choose the Right SRE Metrics for Your System Selecting the right metrics for your system requires careful consideration: Align with business objectives: Metrics should reflect what matters to your business and customers. For example, a high-frequency trading platform would prioritize metrics like extremely high uptime (e.g., 99.999%) over broader measures like reliability growth. Consider your architecture: Metrics like latency, availability, and error rates should be assessed from the user's perspective to ensure they improve user satisfaction and the system's overall dependability. Balance leading and lagging indicators: Use a mix of metrics that predict potential issues (leading indicators) and those that measure past performance (lagging indicators). For instance, tracking error budgets as a leading indicator can help avoid breaches of service-level agreements (SLAs). Start small and iterate: Metrics should be specific to your system’s design. For instance, containerized applications may benefit from metrics like pod restarts or Kubernetes resource utilization. Involve all stakeholders: As your system evolves, revisit and update your metrics to reflect current reliability needs, new technologies, or changing business priorities. Prioritize Actionable Metrics: Choose metrics that not only indicate problems but also provide insights into how to fix them. Metrics like mean time to repair (MTTR) or error rates can guide actionable responses. Benchmarking and Coverage: Ensure your metrics are comprehensive, covering all critical components of your infrastructure. Use them to benchmark against industry standards while maintaining alignment with internal goals. Choosing right SRE metrics Remember, the goal is to have a set of metrics that provide actionable insights, not just data for data's sake. Best Practices for Measuring and Improving SRE Metrics To get the most value from your SRE metrics: Practice Key Action Example/Benefit Implement Monitoring & Observability Use tools like Prometheus, Datadog, Grafana for tracking metrics, logs, and traces. Get real-time system visibility and early issue detection. Set Clear SLOs Define realistic Service Level Objectives aligned with business goals. Example: Set a 99.9% uptime SLO for critical services. Regular Post-Mortems & Improvement Cycles Analyze incidents, identify root causes, and adjust processes. Review trends to improve response and reduce bottlenecks. Automate Monitoring Automate data collection, metric analysis, and incident responses. Example: Auto-remediate memory issues by restarting services. Foster a Blameless Culture Encourage open discussions on failures without assigning blame. Focus on solutions and collective ownership of reliability. Provide Continuous Education Train the team on SRE tools, practices, and techniques regularly. Access resources like SRE books, blogs, and workshops. Encourage Shared Responsibility Promote collaboration between development and operations teams. Adopt a DevOps mindset; developers monitor their apps in production. Following these practices creates a feedback loop that continuously improves your system's reliability. Leveraging SRE Metrics to Enhance DevOps Practices SRE metrics can significantly enhance DevOps workflows by driving data-driven decisions: Inform capacity planning: Use traffic and saturation metrics with tools like AWS CloudWatch or Prometheus to forecast resource needs and avoid bottlenecks. Enhance CI/CD pipelines: Integrate error and performance metrics into deployment pipelines using Jenkins or GitHub Actions to ensure only stable builds are deployed. Drive automation: Define thresholds for key metrics like latency or error rates to trigger auto-scaling or failovers in Kubernetes or AWS. Facilitate better communication: Shared dashboards in tools like Grafana or Splunk align development and operations teams with a common understanding of system health. By embedding metrics into DevOps, you enable a resilient and efficient development lifecycle. Common Challenges in SRE Metric Implementation While implementing SRE metrics, teams often face these challenges: Data overload: Avoid analysis paralysis by prioritizing actionable metrics like the "Four Golden Signals" (latency, traffic, errors, saturation). Alert fatigue : Tackle alert desensitization with best practices like deduplication, grouping alerts, and escalation policies. Metric accuracy: Ensure reliable data collection with consistent sampling intervals and robust error correction mechanisms. Cultural resistance: Combat skepticism with workshops or demos that show how metrics can drive informed decisions and faster resolution times. Tool complexity: Start small, using essential tools like Prometheus and Grafana, before scaling to more advanced stacks. Addressing these challenges requires a mix of technical solutions and fostering a metrics-driven culture. Emerging Trends in SRE Metrics SRE practices are evolving rapidly. Stay ahead with these emerging trends: AI-driven analytics: Tools like Dynatrace and Splunk Observability use machine learning to predict failures and optimize reliability. User-centric metrics: RUM tools like Google Lighthouse and New Relic measure real-time user experience, driving customer satisfaction. Security integration: DevSecOps practices increasingly monitor security metrics like vulnerability scans and threat detection. Distributed tracing : Tools like Jaeger and OpenTelemetry enable end-to-end request tracing, critical for troubleshooting microservices. Chaos engineering: Platforms like Gremlin and Chaos Monkey simulate failures to test and improve system resilience. Adopting these trends helps refine your SRE strategy and ensures your system meets modern demands. Visualizing the SRE Metrics with SigNoz Visualizing SRE metrics is crucial for making informed, data-driven decisions. SigNoz provides an intuitive and unified platform to monitor the Four Golden Signals—Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation—alongside other key metrics. You can set up detailed dashboards to monitor: - Average Latency: Provides a general overview of system responsiveness. Percentile Metrics (e.g., 95th, 99th): Focus on edge cases that might negatively impact user experience. Using SigNoz, you can create alerts for latency thresholds, such as response times exceeding 500ms for critical services. Errors SigNoz provides robust error tracking capabilities, allowing you to: Categorize Errors: Distinguish between client-side, server-side, and third-party issues. Analyze Trends: Identify recurring error patterns over time to proactively resolve issues. Set Error Budgets: Track error rates and ensure they align with your defined error budget policies. With its detailed logs and trace data, SigNoz helps you trace the root cause of errors quickly, minimizing downtime and improving reliability. Saturation Stay ahead of resource exhaustion by monitoring saturation metrics such as CPU, memory, and disk utilization. SigNoz enables you to: Set Resource Alerts: Receive notifications when resources approach critical thresholds (e.g., 80% CPU usage). Custom Dashboards and Alerts SigNoz's custom dashboard capabilities allow you to combine metrics into a unified view. Monitor and Optimize: Use SigNoz's insights to continuously improve system reliability and performance. By leveraging SigNoz, you gain a powerful tool to transform raw data into actionable insights, enhancing both system reliability and user experience. Key Takeaways SRE metrics are essential for maintaining reliable, high-performance systems. The Four Golden Signals provide a solid foundation for SRE practices. Additional metrics like availability, throughput, and MTTR offer deeper insights. Choosing the right metrics requires alignment with business goals and system architecture. Implement best practices like establishing clear SLOs and fostering a blameless culture. Tools like SigNoz can significantly simplify SRE metric implementation and analysis. FAQs What's the difference between SRE metrics and traditional IT monitoring? SRE metrics focus on user-centric, service-level indicators that directly impact reliability and performance. Traditional IT monitoring often emphasizes system-level metrics that may not directly correlate with user experience. How often should we review and update our SRE metrics? Review your metrics at a minimum quarterly. However, in fast-paced environments, monthly reviews can help you stay ahead of emerging issues and opportunities for improvement. Can small teams or startups benefit from implementing SRE metrics? Absolutely. SRE metrics can help teams of any size improve their system reliability and efficiency. title: Office Space Utilization: What It Means and How to Measure It
summary: Learn what office space utilization means, how to measure it, current benchmarks from real portfolios, and how to turn the data into smarter planning decisions.
body_text: Most real estate portfolios are sized for a moment that almost never happens: everyone in, every desk full, every room booked. But the data says otherwise. Across the latest Occupancy Intelligence Index, average utilization sits at just 9-11%, even on days when peak usage climbs to 52-60% of capacity. That gap, between what you pay for and what actually gets used, is where CRE budgets quietly leak. For a real estate leader facing a lease renewal or a headcount forecast, the real question is how much of that space is actually working for you, and when. Utilization shows up differently depending on what you're measuring: Desk utilization : how many workstations are occupied on a given day, not how many are assigned Meeting room utilization : how often booked or open rooms actually hold people Neighborhood utilization : how a team's dedicated zone performs across a full week, not a single snapshot Portfolio utilization : how a building, floor, or region compares against the rest of your footprint This piece walks through what utilization means, how to measure it accurately, the benchmarks worth comparing yourself against, and how to turn that data into a real planning decision. Curious how your portfolio's utilization stacks up against the market? See how 200+ enterprises benchmark peak, average, and midweek attendance in the 2026 Workplace Occupancy & Utilization Index. Download the Index → What Is Office Space Utilization? Office space utilization measures how much of your available capacity gets used, and when, over a defined period. That's a different question than the one most portfolios were designed to answer. Older planning models leaned on static ratios: square feet per employee, headcount divided by desk count, a number fixed at move-in and rarely revisited. Utilization is dynamic. It asks how a floor performs on a Tuesday versus a Friday, how a conference room behaves during a 10 AM crunch versus a quiet Thursday afternoon, and whether the answer changes month over month. What matters is how many of those seats are working for you at the moments people actually show up. For a CRE leader, that reframing changes the decision in front of you. You're managing a resource whose value depends entirely on whether anyone is using it, and most portfolios are paying full price for space they can't see being used at all. How to Measure Office Space Utilization Measuring utilization means comparing occupied capacity to total capacity over time, and doing it consistently across desks, meeting rooms, neighborhoods, floors, and the full portfolio. Get the unit of measurement wrong, or measure only once, and the number will mislead you regardless of how precise it looks. Break the number out by space type and by time window. A desk-ratio problem and a meeting-room shortage call for entirely different fixes, and neither shows up if you only track a blended average. Below, we cover the formula (what counts as "used" and why point-in-time counts mislead), and the data sources, including badge, WiFi, room booking, passive occupancy detection, that feed it. The Utilization Formula and What Counts as "Used" At its simplest, utilization is occupied capacity divided by total capacity, tracked over a defined period rather than a single moment. A floor's utilization on a given day reflects how many of its desks or seats were actually occupied at some point, not how many employees are assigned to it. Point-in-time headcounts mislead because they capture one instant and treat it as representative. A single walkthrough or a monthly badge count can miss the pattern entirely. The distinction between peak, average, and sustained utilization matters here: peak tells you the busiest moment you need to plan for, average tells you the baseline you're paying to maintain, and sustained utilization tells you whether a space holds steady demand or spikes unpredictably. Data Sources for Utilization Measurement Most portfolios already have some version of occupancy data sitting in existing systems: badge and access logs, WiFi or network signals, videoconferencing data, or room-booking platforms, and in some cases passive occupancy detection from area sensors. Each has a real gap. Badge data shows building entry, not which floor or zone someone actually used. WiFi signals estimate people count at the building or floor level with roughly 85% accuracy but can't tell you which desk or room was occupied. Room-booking systems only show what was reserved, not what was actually used, and ghosted bookings routinely inflate the picture of demand. None of those gaps mean you need to rip out what you have. The Meridian platform is built to integrate with whatever occupancy data a customer already has, badge systems, WiFi infrastructure, booking platforms, or area sensors, rather than requiring a single proprietary source. The Large Spatial Model (LSM) is trained on 250M+ sq ft of measured workplace data, and it uses that training to forecast and fill the gaps a single data source leaves behind. That's the practical difference between one occupancy feed and full portfolio coverage. Occupancy Intelligence unifies whatever inputs you already have into one continuous measurement layer, resolving down to desk, room, neighborhood, and floor, so a CRE leader sees utilization at every level of the portfolio rather than a single blended number updated once a quarter. Office Space Utilization Benchmarks and Metrics That Matter Once you're measuring consistently, the next question is what "normal" looks like. A handful of metrics matter more than the rest: peak-day utilization, average utilization, average daily peak, the split between meeting-room and desk utilization, and the difference between midweek and edge-of-week attendance patterns. The current data shows a wide gap between average and peak. Average utilization across measured portfolios runs 9-11%, but peak-day usage reaches 52-60% of capacity, concentrated in the middle of the week. Enclosed collaboration space carries an 18% shortage rate at 2 PM, even though enclosed focus space sits at just 8% of total footprint and runs at 77% occupied capacity, while open focus space, at 69% of footprint, runs at 85% occupied. That combination, low averages, high midweek peaks, and specific space types running short while others sit half-empty, is the pattern behind most mismatched portfolios. You can compare your own numbers against it in the Occupancy Intelligence Index Explorer , built from the same measured dataset. How Utilization Data Drives Better Space Decisions Utilization data is only useful once it changes a decision. That means moving from a report you read to an outcome you own. Below, we look at three of those outcomes: right-sizing the portfolio to avoid lease cost, designing space around how your teams actually work, and running facilities and operations on real usage instead of a guess. Right-Sizing the Portfolio and Avoiding Lease Cost Large conference rooms that mostly host small huddles and desk ratios set years ago that no longer match attendance: these mismatches compound across a portfolio. The fix depends on being able to match the space you keep to the demand you can actually measure, floor by floor and building by building. Real-life example: $18M in lease cost avoidance An Australian financial services firm used occupancy data to right-size its real estate footprint, avoiding $18M in lease costs over three years. The firm measured actual utilization across its buildings and made portfolio management decisions grounded in what was being used, not what headcount projections assumed. That's the pattern behind most successful right-sizing efforts: the decision to exit a lease, shrink a floor, or hold a building comes after the data confirms it. Avoiding lease cost is a byproduct of measuring correctly. Designing Space Around How Teams Actually Work Utilization data also shapes what kind of space you keep. A neighborhood built around a sales team that spends most of its day at desks needs a different mix than one built around a design team running long collaborative sessions. That's a space optimization problem: matching the ratio of desks, enclosed rooms, and open collaboration areas to how a specific team spends its time, verified against measured occupancy rather than a survey people filled out once. More Efficient Facilities and Operating Costs Reliable utilization data has a second, quieter payoff: it tells facilities teams where to spend money on operations, and where to stop. Condition-based cleaning and HVAC optimization are downstream decisions, and they only work if the utilization data feeding them is accurate. Real-life example: $2M in annual cleaning savings A global bank integrated occupancy intelligence with its building operations platform and used the data to align cleaning frequency with actual space usage. The result was a 50% reduction in cleaning costs, worth $2M annually, without a drop in service quality. Deutsche Bank has run a similar playbook across an even larger footprint. Managing a roughly 20-million-square-foot portfolio spanning 4,000 leases, the bank used occupancy intelligence to target cleaning schedules to actual usage and pilot occupancy-driven HVAC automation, achieving energy savings of more than 30% on some days as part of its path to net zero by 2050. Turning Utilization Data Into a Planning Decision Reporting on utilization is not the same as acting on it. The step most portfolios skip is turning a dashboard into a scenario: what happens if you consolidate two floors, sublease a building, expand into a new market, or shift the neighborhood mix on an existing floor. This is where scenario-modeling tools come in. VergeSense's Predictive Planning is one example: built on VergeSense's Large Spatial Model, it lets teams model space demand against measured occupancy patterns before committing capital, rather than defending a plan built on assumptions in a stakeholder meeting. This allows a CRE leader to test a headcount change, a policy shift, or a redesign and see the capacity and experience impact before signing anything. That's the strategic layer utilization measurement is building toward. The data tells you what's happening. Planning tells you what to do about it, and the two only work together when they're built on the same measured foundation. How to Improve Office Space Utilization Improving utilization starts with measuring it consistently. A workable sequence looks like this: Establish a baseline across desks, rooms, and neighborhoods. Compare that baseline against portfolio-wide benchmarks rather than assumptions. Identify where peak and average diverge most sharply. Test changes (a consolidated floor, a rebalanced neighborhood, a different room mix) against the same measured data before making them permanent. The VergeSense platform is built to run that whole sequence: Occupancy Intelligence supplies the continuous measurement that the first three steps depend on, and Predictive Planning powered by the Large Spatial Model handles step four, scoring a proposed change against real behavioral patterns before a wall moves or a lease commits. None of that requires a fresh six-figure study every time a lease comes up. The point of continuous utilization data is that you already have the baseline the next decision needs — and the model to pressure-test the next one against it. Curious how your office space utilization compares to peers? See the latest workplace benchmarks from 200+ enterprises and 250M+ sq ft of measured workplace data in the VergeSense Occupancy Intelligence Index. Read the Report → FAQs About Office Space Utilization What Is a Good Office Space Utilization Rate? A good utilization rate is one where your peak and average track your actual attendance policy, not someone else's benchmark — there's no universal number. Measured data shows average utilization around 9-11% with peak days reaching 52-60%, so "good" depends on space type and goals, not a fixed target. How Is Office Space Utilization Different From Occupancy? Office space utilization is occupancy measured against total capacity over time, rather than a single headcount at one moment. That distinction is what surfaces patterns like peak-day surges or midweek concentration that a point-in-time count can't reveal. How Often Should You Measure Office Space Utilization? You should continuously measure office space utilization, and not at a single point in time. Point-in-time studies capture one moment and go stale before the next lease decision, while ongoing measurement across desks, rooms, and floors lets you track whether patterns are shifting and catch changes before they show up in a renewal negotiation. Can You Measure Utilization Without Installing Sensors Everywhere? Yes, you can measure utilization without sensors in every space. Badge data, WiFi signals, videoconferencing data, and room-booking systems all provide partial signals already, and the VergeSense platform integrates with whatever sources you have, using the Large Spatial Model to fill the gaps those sources leave.

title: Conexon Connect Scales with Agent Workforce Cloud | Calix Press Release
summary: As a subsidiary of rural fiber broadband leader Conexon—which has helped secure more than $2 billion in federal, state, and local grants plus subsidy funding for FTTH projects, supporting fiber deployments nationwide—Conexon Connect is investing in secure agentic AI from Calix to deliver exceptional subscriber experiences that win markets
body_text: Jul 23, 2026 5 min read Conexon Connect Chooses Calix Agent Workforce Cloud To Advance 79 NPS and Scale Their Go-to-Market Strategy As a subsidiary of rural fiber broadband leader Conexon—which has helped secure more than $2 billion in federal, state, and local grants and subsidy funding for FTTH projects, supporting fiber deployments nationwide—Conexon Connect is investing in secure agentic AI from Calix to deliver exceptional subscriber experiences that win markets SAN JOSE, Calif.—July 23, 2026— Calix, Inc. (NYSE: CALX) announced today that Conexon Connect , the internet service provider arm of rural fiber broadband leader Conexon , is leveraging Calix Agent Workforce™ Cloud on the AI-native Calix One ™ platform to scale their growth across residential, business, and multi-dwelling unit (MDU) markets. Since first partnering with Calix in 2021, Conexon Connect has grown rapidly from the ground up, scaling over five years, with current projects across Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Missouri expected to deliver broadband access for nearly 500,000 rural Americans . They have paired that growth with exceptional subscriber loyalty, earning a Net Promoter Score℠ (NPS®) of 79 —more than double the typical broadband industry average. Conexon Connect has leveraged the Calix platform to deliver differentiated experiences to residential subscribers with SmartHome ™—including parental controls, secure connectivity, and outdoor Wi-Fi —and has driven adoption through targeted upgrade campaigns, personalized marketing, and data-driven subscriber engagement strategies. By adopting Agent Workforce Cloud on the Calix One platform, Conexon Connect will now scale and accelerate these winning strategies through secure collaborative AI workflows. As Conexon Connect expands their use of agentic AI, the company continues to benefit from being part of the broader Conexon ecosystem. For more than a decade, Conexon has collaborated with electric cooperatives across 80 markets to launch and deploy fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) networks in their territories, with nearly 50 projects now reaching 100 percent of members. By combining more than $2 billion in funding support with deep expertise across every stage of deployment—from strategy and network design to construction, operations, marketing, and customer support—the company has helped service providers deliver FTTH internet access to more than 4 million rural Americans. John Walburn, chief operating officer at Conexon Connect, said: “ Broadband expansion throughout rural America requires innovative solutions and tools that help our team move faster and serve our partner communities better. With the AI-native capabilities of Calix One, we can unlock new growth opportunities while driving operational efficiency—automating workflows, strengthening our teams’ expertise, and streamlining the key actions that drive subscriber acquisition. That means we can grow smarter, operate more efficiently, and keep connecting rural America at scale.” Michael Weening, president and chief executive officer at Calix, said: “Conexon transformed the economics of rural broadband by helping electric cooperatives build, operate, and scale fiber networks. Together, we have shown that long-term success extends beyond the fiber build—it depends on how effectively providers engage subscribers, market differentiated services, and deliver ongoing value to communities. Conexon Connect has proven that model supported by the Calix platform, driving greater subscriber growth and customer lifetime value through personalized marketing and differentiated subscriber experiences. With Agent Workforce Cloud, Conexon Connect will be able to accelerate those proven strategies across their business in a trusted, secure, and predictable manner. We are grateful for the opportunity to keep innovating together and provide an AI roadmap in Calix One that will enable an expanding return on investment for John and his team.” Learn how Calix One enables service providers to standardize operations and scale AI-driven execution across distributed networks. Calix customers can access the Calix AI Leadership Playbook , explore the award-winning “AI Academy” in Calix University , or register for upcoming Calix Customer Success webinars . About Calix Calix, Inc. (NYSE: CALX) is an AI platform company that enables service providers to transform their operations and accelerate delivery of differentiated experiences—so they can compete and win in the markets and communities they serve. Through the AI-native Calix One platform, service providers can securely and privately activate agentic AI alongside their human teams to acquire new subscribers, grow existing subscriber revenue, and build loyalty across residential, business, municipal, and MDU markets. More than 1,200 customers of all sizes leverage the Calix One platform, which has evolved over 15 years at an investment of more than $2 billion. Calix innovation cycles are underpinned by a strong financial balance sheet and a people‑first culture that routinely earns broad industry recognition—winning 81 culture and innovation awards since 2025 alone, as well as Fortune’s 100 Best Companies to Work For® in 2026.
